PETs Transformer
TrustED PETs Transformer challenge

A privacy release gate.

Tell it who gets the data. It protects the data, proves it is still useful for that recipient, and blocks any release that fails.

Since AI Hackathon 2026Protect the data, keep its value
Open with the one-line promise. Point at the two models: the same hospital data before and after the gate. Everything in this talk comes from the working tool, run on the challenge's synthetic data.
The problem

Removing names is not enough.

Data must be shared with researchers, vendors and the public. Strip too little and people are found again. Strip too much and the data answers nothing.

98.9%

of patients in the challenge's hospital data are the only person with their birth date, sex and postcode.

Too little

Three ordinary columns single out almost everyone. A name was never the only key.

Too much

Coarsen everything and the length of stay, the revisit rate and the trend are gone.

PETs Transformer02
The brief's own words: "Removing names or other obvious identifiers is rarely enough." Our number makes it concrete. The balance is the whole problem, and today teams strike it by hand.
Our answer

Start from the recipient, not the data.

A sharing scenario says who receives the data, how far they are trusted, how many look-alikes each row needs, and which questions they must still answer. Six steps follow, and the last one can say no.

1

Detect

Labels every column from its values and its name. Finds personal data in free text.

2

Select

Keeps only what the questions need, then picks a technique per column.

3

Tune

Searches age bands, areas and time detail against the real question scores.

4

Transform

A key per recipient, rows shuffled, stand-out rows lose one clue at a time.

5

Verify

Attacks the output and asks the questions. Releases, holds or blocks.

6

Report

Every column, every question and every risk that remains.

PETs Transformer03
The bottom row maps our six steps onto the brief's four objectives. The next six slides take the brief's five demonstration points in order. The key design choice: the scenario drives everything. A column no question needs is dropped whatever it contains. And Verify can refuse: a release that breaks a question or leaves a row standing out goes back for another attempt, or is blocked.

Seven roles, each with its own colour throughout the app. A person confirms the columns Detect is unsure about; unsure columns count as private until then. Honest caveat: the name lexicon was written after reading the public catalogue, so 0.86 is optimistic. On values alone, as in the unnamed file, it is 0.65.
02 · Select Demo point 2: PETs per data type

The recipient's questions decide what leaves.

PETs Transformer08 · Self-assessment with pets-eval against its public attackers, not official judging
The public dashboard gets no rows: 254 noisy answers, at most 4 visits per person, budget shared by the square root of each question family's size. That is why we gain most at the tightest budget. Text redaction: 0.17% of identifying values survive in held-out chats. Point at the 0.32: we don't hide it. The scenario needs minute timestamps for its detection rules and sets no look-alike bar, so the gate released it as asked. The unseen file shows the engine on data it has never seen.
Demo point 5 The sharing scenario

Each release is built for one recipient, and says so.

Trust level, look-alike bar and questions come from the scenario: one of the challenge's 27, or a short file anyone can write. The same data comes out differently for each.

Controlled research

University research group

  • Row-level data with coarser clues
  • Every row among at least 5 look-alikes
  • Stable pseudonyms so visits still link
Gets 13 of 53 columns, every row
Partner under contract

AI vendor, contact-centre chats

  • Only what the purpose needs
  • Names, numbers and addresses in text become placeholders
  • Its own key: can't be joined to other releases
Gets redacted chats, usefulness 0.97
Anyone

Public weekly dashboard

  • No rows, ever
  • Noisy answers to a fixed question list
  • A privacy budget that's stated, and adds up across releases
Gets 254 answers at ε 1
PETs Transformer09
This answers the brief's fifth point directly: the evidence opens with who the data is for, their purpose and trust level. A public scenario with no question list is blocked, because there is nothing safe to publish.
Honesty What remains

What we did not solve, measured.

The organisers' hidden attackers weren't available, so the engine runs a stronger attacker of its own and reports what it finds.

Next

  • Noisy answers for a written scenario's questions
  • Protection across a person's repeat records
  • Sign-in, so a team can share one gate

Runs on your machine with docker compose up. No outside service sees the data.

25%

Insider knowledge

Knowing a patient's clue columns singles out nobody. Adding their diagnosis singles out 25% of visits; every kept fact, 98%.

75%

Repeat visits

Of patients with more than one visit, 75% have a unique pattern across them, which a row-level check can't see.

0.32

Security logs

Detection rules need minute-level timestamps, and the scenario sets no look-alike bar.

ε adds

Public answers

The budget is per release: 52 weekly releases at ε 1 make ε 52 a year. The Laplace sampler isn't hardened against floating-point attacks.
